"[Principle] No processing is applied; the original image is displayed directly as the reference baseline.\n[Formula] g(x,y) = f(x,y)\n[Note] Used for side-by-side comparison with the results of the other eight gray-level transformations, showing how each transformation adjusts the gray-level distribution."
② Linear gray-level transformation (Eq. 2-1)

"[Principle] Performs linear stretching/compression on pixel gray levels within a limited range, expanding the dynamic range and unifying the mapping. Suitable for images whose gray levels concentrate in a narrow interval due to under-/over-exposure.
[Eq. 2-1] g(x,y) = [(d-c)/(b-a)] · [f(x,y) − a] + c
[Parameters] This demo: a=50, b=200, c=0, d=255, i.e. stretching [50,200] up to the full [0,255] range.
[Effect] Mid-tone gray levels are stretched apart and overall contrast is enhanced."
③ Image inversion transform (Fig. 2-3)

"[Principle] A special case of the linear transformation: black becomes white and white becomes black, the same as the photographic negative effect. Often used to visualize medical images (such as X-rays) and mask images.\n[Formula] g(x,y) = 255 − f(x,y)\n[Correspondence] The inversion curve shown in Fig. 2-3."
④ Three-segment piecewise linear transform / contrast stretching (Eq. 2-2, Eq. 2-3)

"[Principle] The three-segment piecewise linear transform can stretch one gray-level interval while suppressing the others, highlighting the gray range of interest.
[Eq. 2-2 (clipping form)] Compresses [0,a) to c and [b,Mf) to d, with a linear mapping in between:
 g(x,y) = c, 0 ≤ f < a
 = [(d-c)/(b-a)]·(f(x,y)−a) + c, a ≤ f < b
 = d, b ≤ f < Mf
[Eq. 2-3 (slope form, implemented by this function)] Keeps the slopes of both end segments and only adjusts their magnitudes:
 g(x,y) = (c/a)·f(x,y), 0 ≤ f < a
 = [(d-c)/(b-a)]·(f(x,y)−a) + c, a ≤ f < b
 = [(Mg−d)/(Mf−b)]·(f(x,y)−b) + d, b ≤ f < Mf
[Parameters] This demo: a=60, b=200, c=20, d=230, compressing the low and high values at both ends while expanding the middle tones."
⑤ Clipping (Fig. 2-6, special case of Eq. 2-3)

"[Principle] A special case of the piecewise linear transform. Setting c=0 and d=Mg=255 in Eq. 2-3 suppresses [0,a] to black and [b,Mf] to white, keeping and stretching only the content within [a,b]. Often used to separate the main object from the background.
[Formula] Substituting c=0, d=255:
 g = 0, 0 ≤ f < a
 g = [255/(b-a)]·(f(x,y) − a), a ≤ f < b
 g = 255, b ≤ f < Mf
[Parameters] This demo: a=100, b=180, corresponding to the effect of Fig. 2-6."
⑥ Thresholding (Fig. 2-7, special case of Eq. 2-3)

"[Principle] A further special case of clipping: setting a=b=threshold, c=0 and d=255 in Eq. 2-3 keeps only two gray levels 0/255, producing a binary image.
[Formula]
 g(x,y) = 0, f(x,y) < threshold
 = 255, f(x,y) ≥ threshold
[Parameters] This demo: threshold=128, corresponding to Fig. 2-7."
⑦ Logarithmic transform (Eq. 2-4)

"[Principle] Maps pixel gray levels with a logarithmic function, expanding the low gray range and compressing the high gray range so that the overall gray distribution better matches human visual perception. A typical application is Fourier spectrum display: when the dynamic range of the spectrum is too large, the logarithmic transform brings out the details.
[Eq. 2-4 (PDF)] g(x,y) = a + ln[f(x,y) + 1] / (b · ln c)
 where a, b, c change the starting point and shape of the curve, and +1 avoids taking the logarithm of 0.
[This implementation (common engineering simplification: a=0, b=1, and c solved automatically so the maximum output is 255)]
 g(x,y) = c · ln(1 + f(x,y))
[Parameters] This demo: c=0 (0 means the algorithm computes the optimal scaling automatically)."
⑧ Gamma transform / power-law transform (derived from Eq. 2-5)

"[Principle] Power-law/gamma transforms are used in different display systems to correct the γ response of output devices (i.e. the gray-level curve of CRT/LCD). γ < 1 expands high gray levels and compresses dark areas (enhancing the tonal layers of dark images); γ > 1 does the opposite.
[Eq. 2-5 (PDF exponential transform)] g(x,y) = b^{ c · [f(x,y) − a] } − 1
 Expands the high gray-level interval and compresses the low one.
[This implementation: the standard engineering gamma (power-law) transform] First normalize f as f' = f/255 ∈ [0,1]:
 g(x,y) = c · f(x,y)^γ then map back to [0,255]
[Parameters] This demo: c=1.0, γ=0.5 (less than 1), used to brighten dark areas and expand high gray levels."
⑨ Histogram equalization (Eq. 2-13, Eq. 2-14)

"[Principle] Transforms the gray-level histogram of the original image into an approximately uniform distribution through the cumulative distribution function, increasing overall contrast and making tonal layers clearer. It works notably well on overly bright, overly dark or low-contrast images.
[Eq. 2-13] Discrete gray-level probability:
 pr(rk) = nk / n (k = 0, 1, …, L−1)
 where nk denotes the number of pixels at gray level rk, and n is the total number of pixels.
[Eq. 2-14] Discrete cumulative distribution (equalization transfer function):
 sk = T(rk) = Σ_{j=0}^{k} pr(rj) = Σ_{j=0}^{k} nj / n (0 ≤ rj ≤ 1)
 Maps the original gray level rk to the equalized gray level sk.
[Implementation] Calls OpenCV cv::equalizeHist."
① Show original image

"[Principle] No processing is applied; the original image is displayed directly as the reference baseline.\n[Formula] g(x,y) = f(x,y)\n[Note] Used for side-by-side comparison with the results of the other eight smoothing/denoising methods, showing how each method affects noise and details differently."
② 4-neighborhood averaging (Eq. 2-24)

"[Principle] Neighborhood averaging (2.3.2): the influence of random noise on a single pixel is isolated, so replacing the center pixel with the average gray level of its neighborhood suppresses the noise.
[Eq. 2-23] g(x,y) = (1/M) Σ_{(i,j)∈N} f(i,j)
[Eq. 2-24] g(x,y) = (1/4)·[f(x-1,y) + f(x,y-1) + f(x,y+1) + f(x+1,y)]
[Eq. 2-25] Template H1 = (1/4)·[[0,1,0],[1,0,1],[0,1,0]] (center pixel excluded)
[Effect] Simple and fast; suppresses noise, but edges and details are smoothed at the same time, so the image becomes blurred."
③ 8-neighborhood averaging (Eq. 2-26)

"[Principle] Extends the 4-neighborhood to the 8-neighborhood (including the 4 diagonal directions), so more pixels take part in the average.
[Eq. 2-26] g(x,y) = (1/8)·Σ_{(i,j)∈N8} f(i,j)
 = (1/8)·[f(x-1,y-1)+f(x,y-1)+f(x+1,y-1)+f(x-1,y)
 +f(x+1,y)+f(x-1,y+1)+f(x,y+1)+f(x+1,y+1)]
[Eq. 2-27] Template H2 = (1/8)·[[1,1,1],[1,0,1],[1,1,1]]
[Effect] Smoothing is stronger than with the 4-neighborhood and the image becomes more blurred; the larger the neighborhood radius, the heavier the blur."
④ Threshold neighborhood averaging (Eq. 2-28)

"[Principle] To reduce the blurring effect of neighborhood averaging: a pixel is judged as noise and replaced by the neighborhood mean only when the difference between its gray level and the neighborhood mean exceeds the threshold T; otherwise the original gray level is kept.
[Eq. 2-28]
 g(x,y) = (1/M)Σ f(i,j), when |f(x,y) − (1/M)Σf(i,j)| > T
 g(x,y) = f(x,y), otherwise
[Parameters] This demo: T = 30.
[Note] Too large a threshold weakens the denoising effect while too small a one intensifies blurring; it should be chosen according to image characteristics."
⑤ Median filter 3×3 (Eq. 2-29)

"[Principle] Median filtering (2.3.3) is nonlinear filtering: pixels within a sliding window are sorted by gray level and the middle value replaces the center pixel of the window. Under certain conditions it overcomes the detail blurring caused by linear filtering; it is most effective against impulse (salt-and-pepper) noise and requires no image statistics.
[Eq. 2-29] yi = Med{ f(i-u), …, f(i), …, f(i+u) }, u = (m-1)/2
[Eq. 2-30] yij = Med_W{ Fij } (W is the filter window, here a 3×3 square window)
[Properties] Does not affect step/ramp signals and protects edges; not suitable for images rich in point, line and sharp-corner details."
⑥ 5×5 cross-shaped median filter (Eq. 2-30)

"[Principle] The key of median filtering is the window shape and size (Fig. 2-21). A cross-shaped window suits images containing sharp-pointed geometric structures; the window size usually starts at 3 and then 5, increasing step by step, and should not exceed the size of the smallest object of interest.
[Eq. 2-30] yij = Med_W{ Fij }, with W taken as a cross-shaped window:
 center + horizontal (±1,±2) + vertical (±1,±2), 9 pixels in total, sorted to take the median
[Correspondence] Fig. 2-23f uses exactly this 5×5 cross-shaped median filter (better against salt-and-pepper noise than neighborhood averaging).
[Effect] Strong suppression of salt-and-pepper noise, with slightly more detail loss than 3×3."
⑦ Ideal low-pass filtering (Eq. 2-41)

"[Principle] Frequency-domain low-pass filtering (2.3.5): image edges and noise both lie in the high-frequency part of the frequency domain, so attenuating the high-frequency components removes noise. Pipeline (Fig. 2-27): DFT → multiply by the transfer function → IDFT.
[Eq. 2-40] G(u,v) = H(u,v)·F(u,v)
[Eq. 2-41] H(u,v) = 1, D(u,v) ≤ D0; 0, D(u,v) > D0
[Eq. 2-42] D(u,v) = √(u² + v²) (distance from the frequency point to the origin of the frequency plane)
[Parameters] This demo: D0 = 60.
[Effect] Passes without loss inside the cutoff frequency and removes components completely outside it; the smaller D0, the more thorough the denoising but the heavier the blur, and obvious ringing (Ring) artifacts appear."
⑧ Gaussian low-pass filtering (Eq. 2-46)
⑨ Non-local means (NLM) denoising (Eq. 2-32)

"[Principle] Based on non-local similarity (2.3.4): natural images contain patches at different locations with similar structures; the current pixel value is obtained as a weighted average of all similar patches, with weights depending on inter-patch similarity rather than spatial distance.
[Eq. 2-31] w(i,j) = exp( −d(i,j) / h² ),
 d(i,j) = ‖N(i) − N(j)‖²_{2,α} (Gaussian-weighted Euclidean distance, α is the standard deviation of the Gaussian kernel)
[Eq. 2-32] f'(i) = Σ_{j∈Φ} w(i,j)·f(j) / Σ_{j∈Φ} w(i,j)
[Parameters] This demo: h = 10 (decay control; the larger, the stronger the denoising).
[Extensions] BM3D combines three-dimensional collaborative filtering with non-local similarity; WNNM (Eq. 2-33~2-39) groups similar patches into a low-rank matrix and applies weighted singular-value shrinkage; sparse-representation denoising (Eq. 2-48~2-53, K-SVD) exploits the sparse decomposition over an overcomplete dictionary."
① Show original image

"[Principle] No processing is applied; the original image is displayed directly as the reference baseline.\n[Note] Image sharpening is a family of operations opposite to smoothing: blurring essentially results from averaging or integration, so applying the inverse operations (differentials, differences, gradient operations) makes edges and contours clear; viewed in the frequency domain, blurring means the high-frequency components are attenuated, so high-boost filtering can also achieve sharpening."
② Horizontal-vertical differencing (Eq. 2-56)

"[Principle] Gradient operations (2.4.1): the gradient value is proportional to the gray-level difference of adjacent pixels—large at edges, smaller in gentle areas and zero in uniform areas—so after the gradient operation only the edge points with abrupt gray-level changes remain.
[Eq. 2-54] G[f(x,y)] = [∂f/∂x, ∂f/∂y]ᵀ = [Gx, Gy]ᵀ (gradient vector definition)
[Eq. 2-55] G[f(x,y)] = √(Gx² + Gy²) (gradient magnitude, an isotropic operator; absolute values are commonly used instead to reduce computation)
[Eq. 2-56] Horizontal-vertical differencing: G[f(i,j)] = |f(i+1,j) − f(i,j)| + |f(i,j+1) − f(i,j)|
[Eq. 2-58] g(i,j) = G[f(i,j)] (output gray level equals the gradient magnitude; used by this implementation)
[Note] The last row/column has no direct gradient, so the gradient of the previous row/column is used as an approximation. To keep gentle areas from turning black, threshold-based output is also available (Eq. 2-59~2-62): e.g. g=G (G≥T) / f (otherwise), a fixed background gray level LG, or binary output."
③ Roberts gradient (Eq. 2-57)

"[Principle] The Roberts gradient uses cross differencing (diagonal directions) over a 2×2 window.
[Eq. 2-57] G[f(i,j)] = |f(i+1,j+1) − f(i,j)| + |f(i,j+1) − f(i+1,j)|
[Eq. 2-58] g(i,j) = G[f(i,j)]
[Effect] Strong response to steep edges at 45° and high edge-localization accuracy; but with no averaging factor, noise immunity is poor, and noise, streaks and the like are also enhanced (Fig. 2-32b)."
④ Sobel operator (Eq. 2-63)

"[Principle] The Sobel operator (2.4.2) introduces an averaging factor on top of gradient differencing, overcoming to some extent the problem that gradient sharpening enhances noise as well.
[Eq. 2-63] Gx = [f(i+1,j−1)+2f(i+1,j)+f(i+1,j+1)] − [f(i−1,j−1)+2f(i−1,j)+f(i−1,j+1)]
[Eq. 2-64] Gy = [f(i−1,j+1)+2f(i,j+1)+f(i+1,j+1)] − [f(i−1,j−1)+2f(i,j−1)+f(i+1,j−1)]
[Eq. 2-65] Hx = [[−1,0,1],[−2,0,2],[−1,0,1]], Hy = [[−1,−2,−1],[0,0,0],[1,2,1]]
[Eq. 2-66] g(i,j) = √(Gx² + Gy²); simplified as g = |Gx| + |Gy| to reduce computation (used by this implementation)
[Effect] 1) The averaging factor smooths random noise to some extent; 2) differencing across two rows/columns enhances the elements on both sides of an edge simultaneously, making the edge appear thick and bright (Fig. 2-35)."
⑤ Direct Laplacian sharpening H1 (Eq. 2-70)

"[Principle] The Laplacian operator (2.4.3) is a linear combination of second-order partial derivatives and an isotropic (rotation-invariant) linear operation, responding identically to edges in any direction.
[Eq. 2-67] ∇²f = ∂²f/∂x² + ∂²f/∂y²
[Eq. 2-68] ∂²f/∂x² ≈ f(i+1,j) + f(i−1,j) − 2f(i,j)
[Eq. 2-69] ∂²f/∂y² ≈ f(i,j+1) + f(i,j−1) − 2f(i,j)
[Eq. 2-70] ∇²f = f(i+1,j)+f(i−1,j)+f(i,j+1)+f(i,j−1) − 4f(i,j)
[Eq. 2-71] Template H1 = [[0,1,0],[1,−4,1],[0,1,0]] (variants such as H2~H5 also exist)
[Effect] Direct sharpening enhances edges but the background information disappears (Fig. 2-36). The Laplacian operator also enhances noise, though more weakly than the gradient method; smoothing beforehand is advisable before edge detection."
⑥ Composite Laplacian H6 (Eq. 2-73)

"[Principle] To obtain the Laplacian sharpening effect while retaining background information, the original image is superimposed on the Laplacian sharpening result, giving the composite Laplacian template sharpening.
[Eq. 2-72] g(i,j) = f(i,j) − k∇²f (k relates to the diffusion effect: too large a value overshoots the contour edges, too small a one makes the sharpening unnoticeable)
[Eq. 2-73] With k=1: g(i,j) = 5f(i,j) − f(i+1,j) − f(i−1,j) − f(i,j+1) − f(i,j−1)
[Eq. 2-74] Template H6 = [[0,−1,0],[−1,5,−1],[0,−1,0]]
[Effect] Clear edges while retaining the background gray levels of the original image (Fig. 2-37); the most commonly used Laplacian sharpening template."
⑦ Composite Laplacian H7 (8-neighborhood)

"[Principle] H6~H9 are collectively called composite Laplacian templates (2.4.3). H7 is their 8-neighborhood version, with center coefficient 9 = 1 + 8 (original-image weight 1 plus the sharpening responses of the 8 neighbors).
[Template] H7 = [[−1,−1,−1],[−1,9,−1],[−1,−1,−1]]
[Comparison] H6 = [[0,−1,0],[−1,5,−1],[0,−1,0]] uses only the 4-neighborhood; the same family also includes H8 = [[0,1,0],[1,−3,1],[0,1,0]] and H9 = [[1,1,1],[1,−7,1],[1,1,1]].
[Effect] With 8 neighbors participating in sharpening, the enhancement of edges and textures is stronger than with H6 (Fig. 2-37)."
⑧ Ideal high-pass filtering sharpening (Eq. 2-75)

"[Principle] Frequency-domain high-pass filtering (2.4.4): details such as edges and lines correspond to high-frequency components; high-pass filtering lets the high frequencies pass and suppresses the low frequencies to obtain edge information, and adding the high-frequency edges back to the original image achieves sharpening.
[Eq. 2-40] G(u,v) = H(u,v)·F(u,v)
[Eq. 2-75] H(u,v) = 1, D(u,v) > D0; 0, D(u,v) ≤ D0
[Eq. 2-76] D(u,v) = √(u² + v²) (distance from the frequency point to the origin of the frequency plane)
[Parameters] This demo: D0 = 30; the sharpened image g = f + high-frequency edges (saturated and clipped to [0,255]).
[Effect] H changes abruptly from 0 to 1, which cannot be realized with actual components, and the filtered result shows obvious ringing artifacts."
⑨ Gaussian high-pass filtering sharpening (Eq. 2-79)

"[Principle] The Gaussian high-pass filter corresponds to the Gaussian low-pass filter (Eq. 2-46), with a smooth transition between high and low frequencies.
[Eq. 2-79] H(u,v) = 1 − e^( −D²(u,v) / (2D0²) )
[Parameters] This demo: D0 = 30; likewise the high-pass edges are added to the original image: g = f + high-frequency edges.
[Effect] No ringing; as D0 increases the enhancement becomes more pronounced, and even tiny objects and thin lines remain fairly clear (Fig. 2-41).
[Extensions] Other common high-pass filters: the Butterworth high-pass (Eq. 2-77/2-78, where D0 is defined at the point where H drops to 1/2 of its maximum, with a smooth high-to-low transition and no ringing) and the trapezoidal high-pass (Eq. 2-80, performance between the ideal and the smooth-transition filters; the filtered image has both some blur and some ringing)."
